Chapter 1: Growing Up on the Edge of Nowhere
Picture this: childhood in a tiny, almost forgotten corner of Oregon. It’s nothing like those picture-perfect scenes you see on TV. For a lot of kids here, their whole world is marked by the edges of a trailer park, the far-off sound of highways, and that nagging feeling that life is really happening somewhere else—anywhere but here.
Every day is shaped by the grind of making ends meet, the ups and downs of family moods, and the constant hunt for small moments of happiness tucked inside the ordinary.
Imagine a little girl waking up to her parents fighting in the next room. The walls are so thin, there’s no such thing as privacy—every feeling just kind of bleeds through. Breakfast? Well, it’s whatever you can find in the cupboard. Maybe there’s cereal, maybe it’s just toast. The family’s luck changes with every new job her dad takes, every move to a different trailer park or tiny rental house. It’s like nothing ever really settles down—everything’s temporary.
School ends up being this weird mix of safe haven and battleground. Kids notice the hand-me-down clothes, those shoes that are just a bit too scuffed. There’s a pecking order, and if you come from the “wrong side” of town, you never really forget it. But in the classroom, there are these little escapes—a teacher who really cares, a book that opens your mind, or a project that just lights up your curiosity. Those moments? They might be brief, but they matter.
Back at home, things are complicated. Mom’s doing her best to keep it all together, working hard and trying to raise her kids with almost no help. Dad’s restless—frustrated by all the things that didn’t work out for him—and sometimes, that frustration spills over onto everyone else. The kids learn to read the room, figuring out when it’s safer to keep quiet or slip outside for a bit.
Still, it’s not all hardship. There are moments of real laughter and connection. Siblings turn the backyard into a playground, making up games with whatever odds and ends they can find. Sometimes a neighbor shares a treat, and for a little while, the world feels generous. The local church offers a sense of community, even if the sermons don’t always hit home. Holidays are simple but heartfelt—homemade decorations, a special meal, the excitement of a small gift.
Most people have no idea how much resilience gets built in these early years. Living with uncertainty teaches you to get creative. Having less makes you notice and appreciate the little things. Over time, you start to realize that growing up on the edge of nowhere isn’t just about what you’re missing. It’s about learning how to survive, adapt, and hold on to your dreams for something better.
And then, there’s the 1980s—full of neon colors and pop culture, sneaking into this world through TV and radio. Music videos, sitcoms, and catchy commercials show off a whole different life. You see families in big houses, wearing cool clothes, never worrying about money. For a kid watching from a crowded living room, those images are equal parts inspiring and bittersweet. They spark ambition, sure—but they also make the gap between fantasy and real life feel even bigger.
